name: Alar rim graft

card.summary: A small cartilage graft placed along the nostril rim in rhinoplasty to support the edge, correct retraction or notching and give a smoother nostril outline.
card.aka: Rim graft, articulated alar rim graft
card.note: Surgical technique; outcomes depend on the surgeon and the nose's structure.

quick.overview:
An alar rim graft is a thin strip of cartilage placed along the edge of the nostril during rhinoplasty. It props up the rim so the nostril edge does not pinch, notch or retract upward, giving a smoother nostril outline and a more defined tip.

Surgeons describe it as a simple, effective way to avoid or correct most alar rim deformities. A 2024 series of 317 patients using a modified placement reported favourable results at one year, and other papers describe mono-unit and circumferential variants.
quick.how: It is done by a surgeon during primary or revision rhinoplasty, often through an open approach and frequently together with a septal extension graft that supports the tip. Cartilage is typically taken from the patient's own septum or another site.
quick.risks: Reported complications in the 317-patient series were few, minor and common ones. Revision surgery and residual retraction are the main concerns surgeons address with these grafts.

lead: An alar rim graft is a small cartilage graft placed along the rim of the nostril (the alar margin) in rhinoplasty to support it. The nostril rim contains no cartilage of its own, so grafts are used to prevent pinching, concavity, notching or retraction and to improve outline [1][4].

Postsurgical alar retraction, often following a cephalic trim, is commonly corrected by releasing and repositioning the alar margin, strengthening the tip with a septal extension graft, and supporting the margin with articulated alar rim grafts [1]. The articulated alar rim graft, proposed by Davis, is described as a simple and effective way to avoid or correct most alar rim deformities [3].

A 2001 paper states that for slight retraction an alar rim cartilage graft is an optimal choice, while significant retraction is better handled by other techniques [2]. A 2020 case series describes a mono-unit alar rim graft for pinching, concavity and soft-triangle notching [5], and a 2025 paper uses a circumferential graft for secondary cleft rhinoplasty [6].

chain: Cartilage strip supports the nostril rim
Smoother nostril outline and better-defined tip
angle.text: The graft physically braces the nostril rim, changing how the edge of the nostril sits and how the tip is defined. It is used in rhinoplasty to refine nostril shape and reduce visible rim irregularities.

paras: Alar disharmony is among the most common abnormalities seen after rhinoplasty, and rim grafts are one of the techniques used to eliminate concavity along with lateral crura struts and onlay grafts [2]. Wikipedia notes that rebuilding the alar lobule needs a supporting cartilage graft even though the lobule normally contains no cartilage [7].

The articulated alar rim graft is combined with lateral crural tensioning and a septal extension graft in tip refinement [1][8]. A 2024 modification positions the graft more over the facet polygon and infratip, which the authors say improves tip definition without excess tensioning [3]. The mono-unit version was reported in 29 rhinoplasties [5].

A retrospective series of 317 patients treated with a modified articulated alar rim graft position reported favourable results after a year of follow-up, functional gain for most patients and few minor complications [3]. A series of 29 rhinoplasties used the mono-unit technique [5]. A secondary cleft rhinoplasty series used a circumferential alar rim graft with morphometric measurements [6]. A study of 200 rhinoplasties examined the short nostril [4].
